newsitem.title: USA: Gibson Greetings CEO wants to reinvent the card.
newsitem.headline: Gibson Greetings CEO wants to reinvent the card.

text.p: After four months on the job, Gibson Greetings Inc chief executive officer Frank O'Connell not only wants to reinvigorate his ailing company, he wants to reinvent the whole greeting card industry as well.
He wants consumers to have more choices, including a choice of card brands in supermarkets, drug stores and other retailers that now carry only one brand.
And he wants to make it easier for harried shoppers to find the right card fast, not spend precious time searching card racks.
"To me, the product has become progressively less relevant to the consumer," he said in a telephone interview.
Greeting card selections in supermarkets and other stores "are 180 feet of boring product" that have not changed much in 40 years, he added.
The Cincinnati-based card maker had $388.9 million in sales in 1995, but is a distant third in market share.
Industry estimates are that privately held Hallmark Cards Inc, based in Kansas City, has about 42 percent of the card market and Cleveland-based American Greetings Corp about 36 percent.
Gibson is estimated to have six to eight percent, with much smaller companies splitting the rest.
Gibson, which O'Connell said has lost a bit of market share in the last few years, fired O'Connell's predecessor in February 1996.

Gibson had suffered 1994 derivatives losses then lost several key customers. Early this year, Gibson rebuffed a $290 million bid from rival, American Greetings, citing antitrust concerns. Gibson has said it is no longer for sale.

After a 1994 loss, it returned to profitability in 1995 with earnings of $1.00 a share, excluding results of an unprofitable division which was sold. First Call said analysts expect it to earn $1.20-$1.25 in 1996 and $1.30-$1.40 in 1997.
Gibson's stock closed at $19.125 Friday on Nasdaq. It has risen from about $12 since O'Connell took the helm in August.
McDonald & Co analyst Jeffrey Stein said O'Connell is "a quick study" who has begun addressing problems at Gibson.
"I wouldn't bet against him. He's got some very good ideas and I would bet he's going to succeed -- but not overnight," Stein said.
Stein rates the stock a hold because he does not expect tangible results until the second half of 1997.
"(But) I think investors' patience will be rewarded," he said.

O'Connell headed trading card manufacturer SkyBox International (now part of Marvel Entertainment Group Inc) and also was president of athletic shoe maker Reebok International Ltd's Reebok Brands, North America.

O'Connell said he plans to revamp Gibson's product line, adding "a lot of new products at a high rate of speed" and incorporating new concepts to reach children, teen-agers and "Generation X", the 20- to 30-something age group.

He also wants to sell cards in music and video stores to reach young customers and sell cards featuring dogs and cats in pet food stores and pet departments of mass retailers. Gibson is also studying direct mail catalogs, on-line greetings and other possibilities.
O'Connell said strategic acquisitions may be in the cards, but must be in product areas that make sense alongside the core greeting card business.
